baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Relates the baby boom to child-centred households, consumer markets and psychological ideas about childhood.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Daniel Stoffman describes these arguments in his substantive review; this is named-reader mediation, not a reading of the whole book. He questions how distinctive the cohort itself was.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Interprets Canadian youth politics through the scale and shared culture of the baby-boom generation.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Stoffman reports the interpretation but disputes the space given to radicals and the claim of broad generational sympathy. The qualification is part of this contribution record.

relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Mills's chapter "Québécoises deboutte!"; Hewitt and Sethna on surveillance of women's liberation groups; Owram's "Sexual Revolutions and Revolutions of the Sexes".

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The baby boom as a generation
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Owram's history of the baby-boom generation (1996) is the most-cited work for this group's engaged PhDs and also anchors Canada’s 1960s. Title-level. PhD context: 49 of 107 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Childhood, youth & family in Canada also engage Canada’s 1960s (46%; lift 4.06), counted after removing shared anchors (Owram). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs. Owram's chapters on babies, school days and "the cult of the teenager"; Gauvreau credits Bienvenue with treating youth as a constructed category rather than an anthropological constant.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Canadian political history of party, state and officials
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: A Canadian case of the atlas field: Whitaker's Government Party (contents: "The national Liberal party, 1930–58"; "Party and state in the Liberal era") and Owram's Government Generation (description: intellectuals and the planning of the welfare state, 1900–45) study institutions and the people who ran and justified them. Comparison: the atlas entry is international and methodologically plural; the Canadian field is not presented as a branch of Namier or Tilly.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Postwar national identity and the generation of the 1960s
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Igartua traces English Canada's "other Quiet Revolution" in national identity, 1945–71; Owram moves from intellectuals and the state (1986) to the baby boom (1996). PhD context: 40 PhDs engage both entries (lift 2.5).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Protestant reformers as regulators and as religious actors
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Valverde studies the moral fervour of Protestant social reformers (publisher description); the religion-and-reform entry studies the same churches and social gospel as religious history (Christie and Gauvreau 1996, title-level). The two fields read the reformers differently. In period, Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) asked Valverde's book to 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance', and Christie and Gauvreau (1996, p. xiii, Google Books snippet) said she and Doug Owram used 'a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches'. Those objections concern one book and are recorded on the edge from the mariana_valverde entry (revision 1.136); this field-level edge stays a comparison. Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender order; Cook's Regenerators covers the same reformers' religious thought. Comparison only.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Antimodernism and the invented folk in twentieth-century Nova Scotia (1992, 1994)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1992, 1994). In 'Tartanism Triumphant' (Acadiensis, 1992; pp. 5–9 read) McKay asks how Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century, when 'a collection of hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. His broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9); the narrow answer is the state's cultural power under Angus L. Macdonald. Note 12 takes Lears's definition of American antimodernism and adds the 'simple life' and 'nature'. The Quest of the Folk (1994) is checked at summary and contents level: chapters on 'The Idea of the Folk', Helen Creighton and folklore, Mary Black and handicrafts, the simple life, and the folk 'under conditions of postmodernity'. Muise's review essay (Acadiensis, 1998; pp. 128–32 read) describes the three case studies and quotes the book's conclusion that 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics' (p. 306). Wright's 1995 Acadiensis review essay on English-Canadian intellectual history cites the book for 'a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian' (p. 132 n. 29). A contribution to the field's cultural strand, not its origin: Berger, McKillop and Owram precede it. In the sampled corpus, 56 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. In the Province of History (2010, with Bates) is a later reading.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Canadian imperialism read as one form of Canadian nationalism, through the ideas of its leading spokesmen (1970)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statement (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The introduction opens 'This book is a study in Canadian nationalist thought' (p. 3). Of the earlier critics he writes that 'When critics belaboured imperialism because of its hostility to “Canadian nationalism” what they really meant was that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed. There have been many varieties of Canadian nationalism'; imperialism was 'one variety of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission' (p. 9). His method: 'inquiring into the ideas and ideals which men in the past read into their interpretations of Canada and by exploring the relationship between these conceptions and the environment in which they circulated' (p. 10). The conclusion opens 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism' (p. 259). In-period reception. Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, pp. 274–276, read in full): the book's 'grande originalité' is to conclude that the imperialists were not 'des agents d'une puissance étrangère' but 'de vrais Canadians nationalistes' (pp. 274–275); the thesis, 'déjà suggérée par la monographie de Norman Penlington', 'sera dorénavant très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (p. 275); the book is 'une contribution majeure — sinon un premier modèle — à l'histoire des idées (oui, il y en a) au Canada anglophone' (p. 276). Monet also reports the first criticisms (p. 275 and nn. 2–4): neglect of the economic and military sides of imperialism (Robert Page, JCS 1970), the folding into a Canadianizing ideology of witnesses 'qui seraient plutôt des représentants du pan-britannisme' (Douglas Cole, JCS 1970), and too much weight on 'une petite élite' of intellectuals (H. V. Nelles, Canadian Forum 1970); Page, Cole (1970) and Nelles are not read here. Cole's 1971 comparative article (notes read; body closed) says that Berger 'makes the strongest case for a Canadian nationalistic consciousness within these terms' (n. 33). Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979, read): he 'manages to suspend the reader's initial disbelief and argue persuasively that turn-of-the-century imperialists were really nationalists', but 'Their nationalism and their imperialism were, however, decidedly masculine affairs' (p. 10); intellectual history 'will have to take women into account' (p. 10). Clarence Karr (1989, re-read): Berger 'rescued the previously outcast imperialists and transformed them into significant Canadian nationalists' (p. 161); 'Carl Berger's critics accuse him of an over-Canadianization of imperialism and of ignoring a broader Anglo-Saxon perspective in what Graham Carr refers to as a “scavenger hunt for nationalism”' (pp. 162–163); since his book, group biography 'has been upheld by many historians in Canada as the best method of addressing the Canadian intellectual tradition' (p. 167), and its premise that imperialism can 'only be understood in relation to the characters who espoused it and who came to personify it' risks making thought 'whatever a single advocate chooses to believe' (p. 168). Carr's article (JCS 1982) is checked at its journal abstract only. A contribution, not an origin: Monet credits Penlington with the suggestion. Later reading, not evidence for this edge: Doug Owram's introduction to the 2013 edition (snippet view) calls it 'pretty much the standard interpretation of the way in which Canadian nationalism evolved' (p. xi).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians': class, ethnicity and gender as what Canadians share, and identities as contingent and multiple (1993–2000)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Cook's own words. 'The New History of Atlantic Canada' (Acadiensis 23:1, Autumn 1993, pp. 146–152, read in full) came between Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) and Granatstein's book (1998): 'one of the sweet ironies in the arid debate between “nationalists” and “limited identitarians” on historiography is that neither side appears to recognize that class, ethnicity and gender describe what groups of Canadians have in common, while “nationalism” most often provokes divisions — “regionalism”!' (p. 146). He holds that 'for all the emphasis on differences during recent decades, Canadians from all regions and linguistic groups have, in fact, been growing more alike, at least in aspiration if not in reality' (p. 146). His 2000 CHR forum essay (pp. 260–265 per Buckner's n. 15) is read only in its abstract: the 'limited identities' hypothesis 'has played a major role in the flowering of social history whose dominance is now being called into question by proponents of a renewed “national” approach'; the debate ignores 'the easy assumption that identities, limited or national, are essential rather than contingent', and 'it is too often forgotten that identities are multiple rather than single'. Context: Bliss's abstract (1991–92) asks historians to remember 'that their subject, after all, is Canada' and does not name Cook. Buckner (2000) writes that Cook in 1995 called the phrase 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8; Canada, Quebec and the Uses of Nationalism, 2nd ed., p. 230, unread here). Buckner then groups Bliss, Granatstein and Owram with Careless's later view that the search for limited identities had 'gone too far' (p. 9). A contribution: Cook is a root of the debate (edge 1) and a respondent who in 1993 placed himself outside both camps.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Limited identities and his own early warning against particularism (1969, 1979–81) as the ground of the later fragmentation debate
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (lecture of 1979, Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; read in full, web text). Ten years after 1969 he sees 'a massive outpouring' of writing on regional interests, cultural discords and class disparities in which 'national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted', and says: 'I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood, when he declared “Lord, I know I prayed for rain — but this is ridiculous.”' He disclaims responsibility for the flood ('I scarcely caused the flood') and does not withdraw the concept: 'I do feel the concept has had much value, and still has'. But 'Unity in diversity' now seems rather 'diversity Unlimited', and 'limited identities remain crucial subjects for the historian's regard — but they should not limit his own perception'; 'Now the task is to cut the sight-lines through'. In-period readings: John G. Reid (Acadiensis 16:2, 1987) records that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result', an argument made in Canada by Careless (graph verification note; not re-read here). Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, read): Careless 'too had come to the conclusion that the search for limited identities had gone too far and threatened the very existence of the Canadian nation-state' (pp. 8–9, citing this lecture); 'More recently the same point has been made, somewhat crudely, by Michael Bliss and Jack Granatstein and with greater sophistication by Doug Owram' (p. 9). Buckner contests the premise, calling the 'so-called fragmentation of the historical profession' 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8). An influence as precursor, not participation: his texts predate the 1991–99 exchanges, and no debate text read here names him except Buckner's. Bliss's 1991–92 article (abstract only) does not name him; Bliss is not presented as answering him. edge_814 (cdn_regional → who_killed_debate) stays: it records regional history as the debate's ground.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Postwar Canadian consumption as a politics of nation, class and gender: domestic goods, designers and householders (1999)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the abstract of 'Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada' (ILWCH 55, 1999, a special issue on class and consumption) reads 'How much consumption matters is a cultural difference, a shared national predicament, a politics grounded in the circumstances of class, and learned as a gendered responsibility', and asks 'When producers were not paramount in the regulation of consumption, to what priorities was commerce subsidiary?' Domestic Goods (1999) is unread here; as Brush quotes it (EH.NET, 2000, read in full), it is 'an archeology of the material, moral, and economic choices and constraints which formed Canadian commodity culture in the two decades after the Second World War' (p. 17). It asks 'How much can citizens talk back to manufacturers and the state about domestic goods?' (pp. 3–4). It sets itself against accounts that 'naturalize[d] these hortatory American norms as the intrinsic qualities of "consumer society"' (p. 11), and it places studies of material culture 'into unaccustomed company' (p. 3). Brush notes that Parr 'locates the history of consumption as a history primarily of women as consumers, in contrast to the male-dominated fields of design and manufacturing'. Criticism: Owram (BC Studies 129, 2001, read in full) finds the book's 'strength is in its parts rather than in some seamless thesis' (p. 103). He reads her as arguing that 'the assumption of consumer sovereignty is facile' (p. 104), and answers that 'Canadians, both men and women, preferred Fords to Volvos, and that is what they got' (p. 105). edge_843 (cdn_women_gender ↔ consumption, comparison) is title-level; this edge adds read evidence.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Protestant reformers read as moral regulators rather than as religious actors, and the church historians' objection that this excised the churches from progressive thought (1991–96)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her object overlaps the field's. The book studies Methodist and Presbyterian church organizations, the Salvation Army, the WCTU, the YWCA and the National Council of Women (Dehli 1992, p. 316, read), with familiar reformers such as Chown, Shearer and Woodsworth (Loo 1992, p. 277, read). Her reading is regulatory: purity work 'was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17, quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124), and the discourse of moral reform 'needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' ('Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', 1992, p. 216, read). In-period objections from historians of religion and reform. Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) finds that 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift', suggests Richard Allen's typology of radical, progressive and conservative reformers, and holds that 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'. Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), known here only through Google Books search-within snippets: 'historians such as Doug Owram and Mariana Valverde have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from "progressive" currents of modern thought and social action' (p. xiii); 'Valverde has argued that in early twentieth-century Canada issues such as social purity and immigration were controlled by a hegemonic exercise of power by the state and middle-class organizations' (p. 187), and her analysis 'wrongly posits the view that given the hegemonic influence of the state, there was only one option regarding immigration policy – that of racism and the annihilation of immigrant culture', against which they set 'three divergent strands of opinion on the immigration question' among Protestant clergy (p. 188; n. 95, p. 328, cites her pp. 15, 112, 123–8). Their p. 187 summary attributes to her a state-centred hegemony that her own p. 165 qualifies ('the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'); the disagreement is recorded, not adjudicated. A comparison, as her roster row and edge_861 (moral_regulation – cdn_religion_reform) have it: the criticism runs from the church historians to her, and she did not answer it in a text read here. The dispute is person-level, which is why it is drawn from her entry; edge_861 stays the field-level comparison.
